questions.q: Per this lesson, why doesn't a company using both Azure and AWS get a combined governance surface automatically?
options: Each cloud's governance tooling is self-contained — Azure Policy only sees Azure resources, AWS Organizations only sees AWS accounts, and neither knows the other exists
Azure and AWS share one global policy engine by default
Multi-cloud governance is not actually possible with any current tooling
AWS does not support any governance controls at all
questions.explain: Both clouds have genuinely capable, fully self-contained governance tooling — the work of multi-cloud governance is deliberately connecting those two separate systems.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four places this lesson says multi-cloud governance typically breaks down?
options: Identity
Policy enforcement
Catalogs
Billing currency conversion
questions.explain: The four break points named in this lesson are identity, policy enforcement, catalogs, and audit logs — not billing currency.

questions.q: What is 'policy drift,' as defined in this lesson?
options: When the same governance rule is enforced with different strictness on one cloud than the other, because two parallel rule sets aren't being actively compared
When a cloud provider changes its pricing without notice
When a user's password expires on one cloud but not another
When a company migrates entirely from one cloud to another
questions.explain: Policy drift happens when maintaining two parallel rule sets lets the second one quietly fall behind the first — not through a deliberate decision, but through neglect.

questions.q: According to this lesson's worked example, how might policy drift actually occur at a real company?
options: Azure Policy is tightened to require encryption-at-rest after a security review, but the equivalent AWS Organizations SCP for S3 is never written, and nothing alerts anyone
AWS and Azure automatically synchronize all policy changes with each other
A company deletes all of its cloud resources on both providers simultaneously
An employee manually copies every Azure Policy rule into AWS without any gaps
questions.explain: The example is a rule tightened on one cloud while the equivalent rule is simply never created on the other — a silent gap, not an intentional one.

questions.q: What does this lesson recommend as the practical governance strategy for most real organizations, which usually aren't split 50/50 between clouds?
options: Treat the primary cloud's rules as the source of truth and deliberately translate each one into the secondary cloud's native controls
Invent a brand-new, cloud-neutral abstraction tool that replaces both Azure Policy and AWS Organizations
Ignore governance on the secondary cloud entirely since it holds less data
Migrate all secondary-cloud workloads immediately regardless of cost
questions.explain: The lesson recommends translating the primary cloud's governance rules into the secondary cloud's own native mechanisms, rather than building a one-size-fits-all tool that understands neither cloud well.
